Deprived of the usual resources, the analyst enters into his opponent's state of mind, identifies with it, and often recognizes at a glance the only means—sometimes absurdly simple—of drawing him into a mistake or rushing him into a miscalculation.

Whist has long been recognized as a way to develop what is called the calculating faculty. People of the highest intellectual ability have sometimes shown an apparently inexplicable enthusiasm for it while dismissing chess as trivial. Certainly no comparable activity places greater demands on analytical ability. The finest chess player in the Christian world may be little more than an outstanding player of chess. Excellence at whist, however, suggests the ability to succeed in more consequential situations where one mind competes against another. By excellence, I mean complete mastery of the game, including an understanding of every source of legitimate advantage. These sources are numerous and varied, often lying in regions of thought wholly beyond ordinary understanding. Careful observation produces clear memories, and to that extent a chess player with strong concentration will perform well at whist. Hoyle's rules, based simply on the mechanics of play, are also sufficiently clear and widely understood. A good memory and adherence to “the book” are therefore commonly regarded as everything good play requires. But the analyst reveals his skill precisely where rules no longer apply. He silently accumulates observations and draws conclusions. His companions may do the same, but the difference in how much they learn depends less on the soundness of their reasoning than on the quality of what they notice. The essential knowledge is knowing what to observe. Our player sets no limits on his attention. Although the game is his object, he does not discard conclusions drawn from things outside it. He studies his partner's face, carefully comparing it with each opponent's. He considers how everyone arranges the cards in their hand, often counting individual trumps and honors from the looks their holders give them. As play continues, he notices every change of expression, gathering valuable insights from the different signs of confidence, surprise, triumph, and disappointment. The way someone collects a trick tells him whether that player can take another in the same suit. The manner in which a card lands on the table reveals whether it is a feint. A casual remark or a slip of the tongue; a card accidentally dropped or turned over, together with the player's concern or indifference about concealing it; the counting of tricks and the order in which they are arranged; embarrassment, hesitation, eagerness, or fear—all provide clues to the real situation for a perception that seems almost intuitive.

I then drilled a hole in the end of the keg above the pitcher and fitted it with a soft wooden plug shaped like a cone. By pushing the plug farther in or pulling it out, I adjusted its tightness. After a few attempts, I found the exact position that let water drip into the pitcher below at a rate that would fill it to the brim in sixty minutes. This was quick and easy to work out: I only had to note how much of the pitcher filled in a certain time. With that arranged, the rest of my plan was clear. I set up my bed on the basket floor so that, when I lay down, my head was directly beneath the pitcher's spout. At the end of an hour, the full pitcher would overflow through that spout, which was slightly lower than its rim. The water would fall more than four feet onto my face. Clearly, this would wake me immediately, even from the deepest sleep imaginable.

“It was eleven by the time I finished these preparations. I went straight to bed, completely confident that my invention would work. I was not disappointed. Every sixty minutes, exactly on time, my faithful clock woke me. I emptied the pitcher back through the hole at the top of the keg, attended to the condenser, and returned to bed. These repeated breaks in my sleep bothered me even less than I had expected. When I finally got up for the day, it was seven o'clock, and the sun stood many degrees above my horizon.

“April 3. I found that the balloon had reached a truly enormous height, and the earth's curve looked much more pronounced. Below me, a group of black dots lay in the ocean. They were undoubtedly islands. Far to the north, at the edge of the horizon, I could see a thin, dazzling white streak. I had no doubt that this was the southern edge of the ice covering the Polar Sea. The sight stirred my curiosity greatly. I hoped to travel much farther north and thought I might eventually find myself directly over the Pole. I regretted that, if this happened, my great height would prevent me from examining it as closely and accurately as I wished.

The two ladies were delighted to see their dear friend again. They said it had been ages since their last meeting and kept asking what she had been doing since then. They paid little attention to the rest of the family, avoiding Mrs. Bennet as much as possible, speaking very little to Elizabeth, and saying nothing to the others. Soon they left, jumping up so suddenly that they surprised their brother and hurrying away as though anxious to escape Mrs. Bennet's polite attentions.

Every woman in the family was pleased at the prospect of the Netherfield ball. Mrs. Bennet chose to believe it was being held in honor of her eldest daughter. She was especially flattered that Mr. Bingley had invited them personally instead of sending a formal card. Jane imagined a happy evening with her two friends and their brother's attention. Elizabeth looked forward to dancing often with Mr. Wickham and seeing his story confirmed by Mr. Darcy's expression and behavior. Catherine and Lydia expected their enjoyment to depend less on any one event or person. Like Elizabeth, each planned to spend half the evening dancing with Mr. Wickham, but they would be perfectly happy with other partners too. A ball, after all, was a ball. Even Mary assured her family that she had no objection to going.

“As long as I have my mornings to myself, I am satisfied,” she said. “I don't consider it a sacrifice to take part in an evening gathering now and then. We all have duties to society, and I count myself among those who believe that everyone should have periods of rest and amusement.”

Elizabeth was in such high spirits that she asked Mr. Collins whether he meant to accept Mr. Bingley's invitation, although she rarely spoke to him more than necessary. If he went, would he consider it proper to join in the dancing? She was rather surprised to learn that he had no doubts on that point. He was far from afraid that either the Archbishop or Lady Catherine de Bourgh would scold him for dancing.

“I assure you,” he said, “I certainly don't believe that a ball of this kind, given for respectable people by a young man of good character, can do any harm. Indeed, I have so little objection to dancing myself that I hope all my lovely cousins will honor me as partners during the evening. I should like to take this opportunity to ask you, Miss Elizabeth, especially for the first two dances. I trust my cousin Jane will understand the true reason for this preference and won't take it as any sign of disrespect towards her.”
